lede: A boy who went through a London workhouse while his mother was taken to an asylum, and who grew up to put on baggy trousers, a tight coat, a bowler hat and a cane, and become the most famous face on earth.

ps: Charles Spencer Chaplin was born in London on 16 April 1889 to two music-hall performers. His childhood was one of hunger, the workhouse and his mother's mental illness.

He went to America with a comedy troupe and in 1914 joined Mack Sennett's Keystone film studio, where he created the Little Tramp. Within two years he was the best-paid and best-known entertainer in the world. He wrote, directed, produced, starred in and later composed the music for his own films.

His left-leaning views and private life made him a target in Cold War America, and in 1952 he was refused re-entry. He settled in Switzerland, was knighted in 1975, and died at his home there on Christmas Day 1977, aged 88.
His father, Charles Chaplin senior, was a singer who drank heavily, left the family and died in 1901 aged 38. His mother, Hannah, sang under the name Lily Harley until her voice failed.

ps.t: He said he first went on stage at five, when his mother's voice broke during a show and he was pushed on to sing in her place.
ps.why: From his own My Autobiography (1964); there is no other record of the night.

ps: Poverty sent him and his older half-brother Sydney to the Lambeth workhouse in 1896, when he was seven, and then to a school for pauper children at Hanwell. Hannah was admitted to asylums several times, and from 1905 for good.

He worked as an errand boy, a printer's helper and a seller of flowers, and danced with a clog-dancing troupe, the Eight Lancashire Lads. In 1908 Sydney got him into Fred Karno's comedy company, the best in London, where he learned slapstick and timing.
1910 to 1913: he toured the United States with Karno's troupe. On the second tour he was signed by Keystone.

February 1914: in only his second film, Kid Auto Races at Venice, the Tramp appeared: too-big trousers and shoes, too-small coat, bowler hat, cane and a little moustache. He made about 35 films for Keystone that year, soon directing them himself.
1915 to 1917: he moved to Essanay, then Mutual, which paid him 670,000 dollars a year. Short films like The Tramp, Easy Street and The Immigrant gave the character his sadness as well as his kicks.
1919: with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith he founded United Artists, a company owned by the artists themselves.

1921 to 1931: The Kid, The Gold Rush and City Lights. Talking pictures arrived in 1927, but he kept the Tramp silent, adding music and sound effects. City Lights, a silent film in 1931, was a great success.
1936: Modern Times, the Tramp's last film, in which audiences heard Chaplin's voice for the first time, singing a song in made-up words.

1940: The Great Dictator, his first true talking picture, mocked Hitler as 'Adenoid Hynkel'. He began it in 1937, while many in America still wanted no quarrel with Germany. He later said that had he known of the death camps he could not have made fun of the Nazis.

1943 to 1945: the actress Joan Barry brought a paternity suit against him. Blood tests showed he could not be the father, but California courts did not then accept such tests as proof, and a jury ordered him to pay child support. In 1944 he was tried and acquitted on a related federal charge. The same year, 1943, he married Oona O'Neill.

September 1952: he sailed for London to open Limelight. At sea he learned the US Attorney General had revoked his permit to return. He settled at Corsier-sur-Vevey, near Lake Geneva, and did not go back to America for twenty years.
April 1972: he returned to Hollywood to receive an honorary Oscar and was given one of the longest standing ovations in the history of the ceremony.
The Kid (1921). His first feature, about the Tramp raising an abandoned baby, starring the child actor Jackie Coogan. It mixes slapstick with real grief.
The Gold Rush (1925). The Tramp in the Klondike: the starving cabin where he cooks and eats his boot, and the scene where he makes two bread rolls on forks dance like feet.

City Lights (1931). The Tramp falls in love with a blind flower seller and helps pay for an operation to give her back her sight. Its last scene, when she recognises him by touch, is often called one of the finest in film.
Modern Times (1936). The Tramp as a factory worker, swallowed into the gears of a huge machine: a comedy about the Depression and the assembly line.
The Great Dictator (1940). It ends with Chaplin, as a Jewish barber mistaken for the dictator, speaking directly into the camera for several minutes in a plea for kindness and democracy.
Limelight (1952), about an ageing music-hall clown, with a scene with the silent comedian Buster Keaton. He also wrote My Autobiography (1964).
Hannah Chaplin (1865 to 1928), his mother. He brought her to California in 1921, where she lived in comfort until her death.
Sydney Chaplin (1885 to 1965), his half-brother, protector, and later his business manager.
Mack Sennett (1880 to 1960), the head of Keystone, who first put him on film.
Mary Pickford (1892 to 1979) and Douglas Fairbanks (1883 to 1939), stars and his partners in United Artists.

His wives: Mildred Harris, married in 1918 when she was 16 and he was 29; Lita Grey, married in 1924 when she was 16 and pregnant, and he was 35, with a bitter, public divorce in 1927; the actress Paulette Goddard, his co-star in Modern Times; and Oona O'Neill (1925 to 1991), daughter of the playwright Eugene O'Neill, whom he married in 1943 when she was 18 and he was 54. That marriage lasted until his death, and they had eight children.

He arrived in the film business just as Hollywood was becoming its capital and the feature film was being born. Silent films could be understood anywhere, which is why the Tramp became famous across the whole world.

The arrival of sound in the late 1920s ended many silent careers. Later, the Cold War and the Red Scare made Hollywood a place of suspicion, where actors and writers were questioned about their politics.
The Tramp, a poor man with a gentleman's manners, is still one of the most recognised figures in the world. Directors and comedians from Jacques Tati to Rowan Atkinson have been influenced by him.
He showed that one person could control a film from script to music. Several of his films are on lists of the greatest ever made, and his home in Switzerland is now a museum, Chaplin's World.

ps.t: In March 1978, two months after his burial, his coffin was stolen from the cemetery at Corsier-sur-Vevey by two men who demanded a ransom. Police caught them and the body was recovered about eleven weeks later.
ps.why: Widely reported at the time; the men were convicted.

myths.c: Chaplin once entered a Chaplin lookalike contest and lost.
myths.t: Newspapers in the 1910s and 1920s told this story in several versions, with him coming third, or twentieth, or not even making the final. No reliable first-hand account has been found.

He never joined any communist party and said so repeatedly. He did support causes like aid to the Soviet Union in the Second World War, and the FBI kept a large file on him. The decision to bar him in 1952 came amid McCarthy-era pressure and anger at his private life.

myths.c: Chaplin and Hitler were born in the same week.
myths.t: Chaplin was born on 16 April 1889 and Hitler on 20 April 1889, four days apart. Both wore a small toothbrush moustache, a likeness Chaplin used in The Great Dictator.

myths.c: Chaplin was born in a gypsy caravan in the Midlands.
myths.t: No birth certificate for him has ever been found. A letter found in his desk after his death, sent in the 1970s, claimed he was born in a caravan near Birmingham. Most biographers still think he was born in south London, as he believed.
